data.title: Take a Ridge-top Walk to Sunset Point
data.shortDescription: Visitors to Mammoth Cave National Park Marvel over the Green River Valley while visiting the popular overlook, Sunset Point.

images.altText: A winter view above a river valley

data.seasonDescription: Many visitors enjoy visiting Sunset Point during peak foliage times in the spring and fall.
data.accessibilityInformation:
The Heritage Trail is appropriate for all visitors and all ranges of mobility.

The first .5 miles of the trail is a raised, wooden walkway, accessible by low grade ramps at the beginning for the trail. The remaining .1 mile of the trail is a flat, stable cement loop, also appropriate for all visitors.

The trail is approximately 6 feet wide with, railings available and benches readily available.

There are waysides along the trail, though they do not offer braille and audio options.

Accessible parking is available alongside the Lodge at Mammoth Cave, within 100 yards from the trail.

Service animals are welcome along this trail.
data.petsDescription: Owners must keep pets on leashes no longer than 6 feet and clean up after their pets.
data.locationDescription: Sunset point is the endpoint of the Heritage Trail, located on the South Side of the park, across the pedestrian bridge from the Mammoth Cave Visitor Center.
data.longDescription:
Above the winding underground passages of Mammoth Cave, you can gaze over the hills and valleys that make up our Kentucky karst landscape.

Take an easy stroll to Sunset Point to enjoy a park-favorite panorama of the Green River Valley where you can catch the best views of fresh spring foliage and vivid autumn colors.
data.durationDescription:
This is a .6-mile (1 km) out-and-back trail that begins and ends at the same trailhead.

As the trail is located very close to the visitor center, it is a great hike to do between ranger programs and scheduled cave tours.

data.title: Birding Seawall
data.shortDescription: Seawall provides great birding opportunities on the west side of Mount Desert Island at Acadia National Park.

images.altText: A black guillemot waits to dive underwater for food

data.longDescription: Seawall Picnic Area is an excellent place inside Acadia National Park to scan for passing seabirds from sandpipers to pelagic species. Any time of the year is a good opportunity to scan with your binoculars or scope, but especially during August and September for southern-bound ducks, grebes, sandpipers, terns, and gulls. The Picnic Area provides an open view of the Great Harbor along with the Cranberry Isles where traveling Northern Gannet or Bald Eagle can be spotted as well. Additionally, nearby Seawall Campground and Hio Road offers the only accessible location to explore the edge of the Big Heath within Acadia.

data.title: Birding Isle au Haut
data.shortDescription: Explore this downeast offshore island that is home to spruce-fir forests, rocky coastlines along with a variety of songbirds, shorebirds, and terns.

images.altText: Birds fly above water near coastline

data.longDescription: Isle au Haut is the least visited part of Acadia National Park by birdwatchers yet a unique feature of the Park. The 8,000-acre island—3,200 acres of which are part of Acadia—is just off the shores of Stonington, Maine. Although the island has a low variety of breeding songbirds because of its mono-landscape dominated by Red Spruce and Balsam Fir, it is ideally located as a migratory stopover for a variety of warblers, shorebirds, and terns. This means the best time to visit the island is May or August. Lastly, the island is accessible only by ferry, this allows the ideal opportunity to scan the waters for Northern Gannet, Black Guillemot, Common Eider among other sea ducks and pelagic birds.

data.title: See Fort Rosalie
data.shortDescription: Discover how the town of Natchez came to be as you explore Fort Rosalie.

images.altText: View of the Mississippi River from Fort Rosalie

data.location: 500 block of South Canal Street, Natchez, MS 39120
data.accessibilityInformation: Accessible picnic tables are available. Wayside exhibits can be viewed from sidewalk.
data.ageDescription: All ages are welcome, however minors should be accompanied by an adult.
data.timeOfDayDescription: Fort Rosalie is open daily from dawn to dusk.
data.locationDescription: Pedestrian entrance is at the corner of South Canal and Green Street
data.longDescription: Discover how the town of Natchez came to be as you explore the wayside exhibits at the Fort Rosalie site. Enjoy a picnic in view of the remains of the fort that was the backbone to a European settlement that survived three different periods of European rule over the course of the 1700s (French, British, Spanish) and became the capital of the Mississippi Territory under United States governance at the end of the century.

data.title: Cultural Demonstrations
data.shortDescription: From April through October, visitors can learn from cultural demonstrators.

images.altText: Stone bison

data.seasonDescription: Cultural demonstrations are available daily between Memorial Day and Labor day; they are available on weekends during the shoulder seasons on either side of the holidays listed (April - October.
data.accessibilityInformation: A limited supply of complimentary wheel chairs are available for visitors with mobility issues.
data.petsDescription: Service animals trained in a specific task are the only animals permitted in the Visitor Center.
data.timeOfDayDescription: Available during the hours of the Visitor Center's operation (8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.).
data.activityDescription: From April through October, cultural demonstrators teach visitors about the craftsmanship of pipestone carving, the practice of quarrying, and the meaning of the stone and the site.
data.longDescription: Visitors to the park from April through October have an opportunity to learn about pipestone craftsmanship and quarrying from American Indian carvers and quarriers!
data.durationDescription: Cultural demonstrators are available throughout the day during the summer season. There is no formal program or set schedule for their demonstrations. Visitors are free to ask questions and talk with demonstrators at their leisure.

data.title: Outdoor Programs
data.shortDescription: Visitors are offered a chance to hear stories about Pipestone's history, learn more about its cultural and natural resources, attend night sky viewings, engage in interactive archeology programs, and more.

images.altText: A ranger at a table outside with families

data.seasonDescription: Guided, formal programming occurs between spring and fall. Although snowshoeing is encourage during the winter months, it is largely self-guided and not formal.
data.accessibilityInformation: For tours around the Circle Trail, please be advised that while the trail is not American Disabilities Act (ADA)-compliant, it may be wheelchair accessible with some assistance (see Accessibility).
data.ageDescription: All ages are welcome at formal programs and events. For tours around the Circle Trail, keep in mind it is a 3/4-mile, paved trail, but can be very hot in the summer.
data.petsDescription: All pets are allowed on the grounds and at most formal, outdoor events/tours, but must be kept under control and on a 6' leash. There are complimentary waste bags at the trailhead to clean up after your pets.
data.timeOfDayDescription: All tours are conducted during the day time. Events such as the night sky viewing and luminaria/music program take place in the evenings.
data.feeDescription: Admission and all programming is free.
data.activityDescription: Guided ranger programs are available during the summer season when staffing allows and range from 30 minutes to 1 hour. Special events are also available for free throughout the year and average 1 hour in length.
data.longDescription: Guided tours and special outdoor events take place between spring and fall. They are all free and open to the public.
data.reservationDescription: No reservations required for outdoor programming.
data.durationDescription: All formal programming varies in time from 30 minutes to 1 hour.

data.title: Winter Snowshoeing
data.shortDescription: Snowshoeing around the Circle Trail is available after January 1st as long as the conditions allow for it.

images.altText: A snowshoe in the snow

data.seasonDescription: Available after January 1st (conditions permitting) until the snow melts.
data.accessibilityInformation: The trail is not ADA compliant, and when covered in snow can be difficult to navigate.
data.ageDescription: There is no age requirement; the only limiting factor is ability. Snowshoeing is a strenuous activity, please give yourself plenty of time (at least an hour) if trying it for the first time.
data.petsDescription: If snowshoeing with a pet, please keep them on a 6' leash at all times and clean up after them (complimentary waste bags are available at the trailhead).
data.timeOfDayDescription: Last snowshoe rental is a 4:00 p.m. and snowshoes must be returned by the time the Visitor Center closes at 5:00 p.m. If bringing your own snowshoes, the trail does not close and you may hike after operating hours.
data.feeDescription: Admission and snowshoe checkout are free (snowshoes are limited).
data.activityDescription: A 3/4-mile snowshoe hike around the Circle Trail. Call ahead to verify snowshoe availability if you'd like to check a pair out for free (first-come, first-served) and to learn more about the current trail conditions.
data.longDescription: Shake off the cabin fever and take advantage of Minnesota's winters on the Circle Trail. Bring your own pair of snowshoes or check out a pair for free in the Visitor Center (limited supply)!
data.reservationDescription: If checking out snowshoes, there is a limited supply available on a first-come, first-served basis (they may not be reserved over the phone).
data.durationDescription: The trail is 3/4 of a mile. Time to complete the hike varies depending on factors such as experience, fitness, and whether visitors stop for photos and to read interpretive wayside signs.

data.title: Walk the Trails and Tour the Mission Grounds
data.shortDescription: Walk the grounds and stand where history happened. Spot wildlife flitting from tree to tree, hiding in the grass, or sunning on the trail. Reflect while surrounded by an expansive view of the Walla Walla Valley. Groups can tour the grounds on their own or with a ranger. The site includes one mile of paved trails and a short stretch of unimproved trail along the historic Oregon Trail. To ensure the safety of all visitors, we ask that you do not bike, skate, skateboard, or rid

images.altText: trail passing an informational sign with a monument on a hill in the background

data.accessibilityInformation:
There are about 1 mile of paved trails available. The trail to the Whitman Monument at the top of the hill is very steep. Benches are available halfway up the hill and at various stopping points around the mission grounds. 

The trail that runs along the historic Oregon Trail is unimproved and uneven.
data.petsDescription: Pets are allowed on leash.
data.feeDescription: Whitman Mission National Historic Site does not collect fees.
data.longDescription:
Walk the grounds and stand where history happened. Spot wildlife flitting from tree to tree, hiding in the grass, or sunning on the trail. Reflect while surrounded by an expansive view of the Walla Walla Valley. 

Informational wayside signs line the trail throughout the site providing context for what you see. On the Mission Grounds Loop, you will find the footprints of the historic mission buildings, the restored mill pond and irrigation system, and restored apple orchard. At the base of the hill lies the burial site of those who were killed in the attack on the mission as well as William H. Gray, his wife, and others who lived in the area. A beautiful view of the surrounding area will greet you along with the Whitman Monument when you reach the top of the hill. 

Before beginning your walk, don't forget to stop by the visitor center to grab a brochure with a map of the park!

To ensure the safety of all visitors, we ask that you do not bike, skate, skateboard, or ride a scooter on the trails.
data.reservationDescription: Self-guided walks are always available. For a guided walk, please check our calendar, email us, or call 509-522-6360.
data.durationDescription: The Mission Grounds Loop is .5 mile long and can be completed in 15 minutes for a quick visit. Additional trails are available for a longer visit.

data.title: Picnic at Whitman Mission
data.shortDescription: Enjoy a picnic at the Whitman Mission picnic shelter. The picnic shelter is available whenever the park grounds are open unless otherwise noted. Please refrain from picnicking outside of the picnic area.

images.altText: Picnic shelter surrounded by trees and grass

data.accessibilityInformation: The path to the picnic shelter as well as the picnic area itself are paved. Wheelchair accessible tables are available.
data.petsDescription: Pets must be on a leash.
data.longDescription:
After walking the trails and touring the museum, enjoy a picnic at our picnic shelter! The picnic area is also a great place to play games like frisbee or catch. Out of respect for the events that happened here, please refrain from picnicking or playing games outside of the picnic area. 

Charcoal grills are available for you to use. Please practice fire safety when using the grills. Fires must be in a grill or a container that will not damage the table, trees, grass or other park resources. Fires and other heat sources must be extinguished and completely cold before any materials are placed in park trash cans. Coals or other combustible materials should never be thrown into the vegetation.
data.reservationDescription: The picnic shelter is available on a first come basis and cannot be reserved.

data.title: Tour the Avery Research Center
data.shortDescription: The Avery Normal Institute (now called the Avery Research Center) was founded by Francis Lewis Cardozo. It was the first secondary school for African Americans in the city of Charleston. The center is now part of the College of Charleston.

images.altText: The Avery Normal Institute in 1870, surrounded by picket fence.

data.longDescription:
Founded by Francis Lewis Cardozo, the Avery Normal Institute was the first secondary school for African Americans in the city of Charleston. A “Normal” school is one that trains teachers.

 

At the end of the Civil War in 1865, Cardozo wanted to establish an educational institute to teach newly freed African Americans. Under slavery, enslaved people were not allowed to read or write. Cardozo recognized that in order to be successful as newly freed people, African Americans needed educational opportunities.

 

After Cardozo received a $10,000 grant from the estate of Reverend Charles Avery, construction on the school began in 1867. The school was designed in the Italianate style with an arched entry, cupola, and piazzas running the length of the building and opening into classrooms. Further financial assistance was received from the Freedmen's Bureau, local merchants, and the American Missionary Association of New York City, who also staffed the school.

 

Operated as a private institution, the Avery Normal Institute served Charleston's most prominent African American families. Many of the teachers at the school were from the local black community and were former students themselves. By 1900, enrollment had reached nearly 500. In 1947, the institute became a public city school.

 

Currently known as the Avery Research Center for African American History and Culture, the center is part of the College of Charleston.

 

Explore More!

  • Tour the museum located in the research center, or participate in an educational program.

  • The Avery Research Center also features a permanent exhibit of a recreated nineteenth century classroom. Experience what it was like attending school over 100 years ago.

data.title: Discover the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor
data.shortDescription: The Gullah-Geechee people are the descendants of enslaved people from west and central African countries such as Angola, Senegambia, and the Gold Coast. Despite their bondage, enslaved people continued to observe and celebrate their culture and heritage. Many enslaved communities also created new customs and traditions in America. The Gullah-Geechee people, for example, are known for their sweetgrass baskets.

images.altText: A close up of a someone's hands weaving a basket out of sweetgrass.

data.longDescription:
The Gullah-Geechee people are the descendants of enslaved people from west and central African countries such as Angola, Senegambia, and the Gold Coast. Despite their bondage, enslaved people continued to observe and celebrate their culture and heritage. Many enslaved communities also created new customs and traditions in America. The Gullah-Geechee people, for example, are known for their sweetgrass baskets. Sweetgrass, found in the southeast coastal region, was used to weave ornate baskets for storing or carrying food and personal items. Today, descendants continue this tradition of basket-weaving and it is now an art. Locals sell these baskets in different parts of the region, including at Market Hall, Charleston’s city center. In the late 1700s, Charles Pinckney, a slave owner and a signer of the Declaration of Independence, gave part of his land to establish Market Hall. Locals and tourists will not only find sweetgrass baskets at Market Hall, they will also find other shops and businesses that contribute to the culture and vibrancy of the city.  

 

To preserve and protect the rich heritage of the region, Congress designated the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor in 2006, which spans the coast from North Carolina to Florida. Hundreds of natural and cultural sites are included in this 12,000 mile stretch of land. Members of the public are encouraged to explore the sites and celebrate the culture of the Gullah Geechee.

 

 

Explore More!

  • After exploring the city of Charleston, take a trip to the Penn Center, located on St. Helena Island. Located fifteen minutes from the National Park Service’s new Reconstruction Era National Monument in Beaufort, SC, the Penn Center is just one of the sites in the area that interprets the events of Reconstruction. Once a school for formerly enslaved people, the Penn Center is now a heritage and education facility dedicated to telling the story of the Gullah-Geechee people. Take a tour of the museum, visit the gift shop, and enjoy the peaceful surroundings of the island.

  • Located 25 minutes outside Charleston, the Caw Caw Interpretive Center also offers interactive exhibits about the Gullah-Geechee people. In addition to hiking the nature trails or strolling along the boardwalk, visitors can tour the rice fields were enslaved people once labored. Guests can also see sites associated with the Stono Rebellion of 1739, one of the largest uprisings of enslaved Africans in North America.

data.title: Do the Junior Ranger Program
data.shortDescription: The Junior Ranger program helps kids get involved and learn more about Ulysses S. Grant's life and times. Anyone can become a Junior Ranger by completing activities during a park visit.

images.altText: children taking a pledge in the foreground with a Park Ranger standing in the background.

relatedParks.fullName: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
relatedParks.name: Ulysses S Grant

tags: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
data.accessibilityInformation: Contact the park at 314-842-1867 or ask to speak with a Ranger while visiting to address any accessibility-related needs while working on the Junior Ranger Program. We are happy to help.
data.petsDescription: Service animals are permitted anywhere in the park, including the historic house. All other pets are not allowed in any building on the property. A service animal is defined as “any dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability”. Dogs are the only animals that can be used as a service animal except for miniature horses.
data.longDescription:
Are you interested in Ulysses S. Grant and the American Civil War? Do you find presidential history fascinating? Do you want to learn more about women's history, slavery, and life on a 19th century farm? The Junior Ranger Program helps students of all ages learn more about Ulysses S. Grant's life and times. While the program is geared for students between the ages of 5 and 14, anyone can work on the activity books, become a Junior Ranger (or perhaps a Senior Ranger!) and earn a badge.

You can get a free, age-appropriate Junior Ranger Activity book from the front desk inside the park's Visitor Center. Three different books are offered (ages 5-7, ages 8-10, and ages 11+), and a park bingo sheet is offered for children under the age of five. Follow the activity instructions in the activity book while visiting the park. When the activity book is complete, return to the Visitor Center to receive your official Junior Ranger badge for Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site. 

If want to learn from home and earn a "virtual" Junior Ranger badge, go to the "Be a Junior Ranger" page of this website.
data.durationDescription: Prospective Junior Rangers and their families should budget 60-90 minutes to watch the film, tour White Haven, walk through the museum, and completed the required number of activities in the Junior Ranger book.

data.title: Stop By The Visitor Center
data.shortDescription: Start your experience at the Visitor Center. Park Staff and volunteers will be located at the front desk to greet you and answer questions. Allow yourself at least a few minutes to become oriented to the park operation. The Visitor Center is open daily from 9:00AM to 5:00PM.

images.altText: building interior with yellow walls and blue carpeting.

relatedParks.fullName: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
relatedParks.name: Ulysses S Grant

tags: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
data.accessibilityInformation: The park's Visitor Center is fully accessible with wheelchairs, walkers, and other assisted mobile devices. The park also owns two wheelchairs that are kept in the Visitor Center and available for use upon request. The park brochure is availble in braille and in German and Spanish. All are availble upon request at the front desk. Assisted Listening Devices and Descriptive Listening Devices are also available upon request for visitors who choose to watch the orientation film in the Visitor Center theater.
data.petsDescription: Pets are not allowed in the Visitor Center with the exception of service animals. A service animal is defined as “any dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.” Dogs are the only animals that can be used as a service animal except for miniature horses.
data.locationDescription: The Visitor Center directly connected to the site's parking lot and roughly 50 yards from the park entrance at Grant road.
data.longDescription:
Start Your Experience at the Visitor Center

The Visitor Center is your entrance into the visitor experience at Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site. Park staff and volunteers (VIPs) will be located at the front desk to greet and orient you to the park. All guided tours of White Haven begin in the Visitor Center and the site's orientation film is shown in the theater every 30 minutes at the top and bottom of each hour. Children interested in earning their Junior Ranger Badge can learn about more the program and pick up an activity book. Temporary exhibits on Ulysses S. Grant's life are also displayed in the Visitor Center on an occassional basis. Restroom facilities and a drinking fountain are also located near the front desk. While exploring the Visitor Center, pick up a brochure with the park map.

Bookstore and National Parks Passes

Books, educational materials, and other gifts are available for purchase inside the Visitor Center. The bookstore inventory is managed Jefferson National Parks Association. Park staff also issue a host of federal recreation lands passes, also known as "America the Beautiful Passes." Annual, Senior Annual, and Lifetime Annual passes are sold, while Active Military, Access, and 4th Grade passes are issued for free upon request. Learn more by visiting the America The Beautiful Passes website.

data.title: Check Out the Park Museum
data.shortDescription: The park museum is housed in a historic horse stable designed by Ulysses S. Grant and completed in 1872. This space is self-guided and there's no wrong way to explore the fascinating content with the museum's six permanent exhibits.

The text for the museum's exhibits does not have a braille translation at this time, although a braille booklet at the front desk includes a translation of the park's brochure and is available upon request. None of the current exhibits include audio tracks or other sounds at this time. Pets are not allowed in the museum except service animals. A service animal is defined as “any dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.” Dogs are the only animals that can be used as a service animal except for miniature horses.
data.petsDescription: Pets are not permitted in the museum except in cases of a service animal. A service animal is defined as “any dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability”. Dogs are the only animals that can be used as a service animal except for miniature horses.
data.locationDescription: The park museum is located in a historic horse stable adjacent to the visitor center. A short paved walkway roughly ten feet long runs between the museum and visitor center and provides easy access to both attractions. The historic horse stable is roughly 200 feet long.
data.longDescription:
An In-Depth Look at Ulysses S. Grant's Life and Times

Located inside the park's 1872 horse stable is a self-guided museum with six permanent exhibits. "An Intricate Tapestry: Ulysses and Julia Grant" examines the life and times of a loving couple that maintained a committed marriage for thirty-seven years. Half of the museum focuses on Ulysses S. Grant's private life, including his relationship to his wife, children, extended family, and close friends. The other half focuses on his public service to the United States, including his service in the Mexican-American War and American Civil War, and two terms as President of the United States. Numerous interactive components also examine the Grants' world tour (1877-1879) and address personal challanges Grant faced during his lifetime.

As the park staff is fond of telling visitors on site, "you could spend two minutes or two days checking out the museum!" When it comes to a time committment, there is no wrong way to explore this space.
data.durationDescription: The museum is self-guided, so individual visitors spend a wide range of time in this space, from just a couple minutes to an entire day. On average, most visitors spend about 20 to 30 minutes exploring the museum.

data.title: Watch the Orientation Film
data.shortDescription: A 22-minute orientation film provides insights into Ulysses S. Grant's military service during the American Civil War and his two terms as President of the United States.

images.altText: man with a beard wearing a suit circa 1870.

relatedParks.fullName: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
relatedParks.name: Ulysses S Grant

tags: Ulysses S Grant National Historic Site
data.accessibilityInformation: An accessible entrance on the east side of the park theater is provided for people who use wheelchairs, walkers, and other assisted mobility devices. The orientation film is shown with open captions. For people with hearing impairments, Assistive Listening Devices (ALD) are available for film presentations upon request. Furthermore, the theater is also equipped with an induction loop for visitors with T-coil enabled hearing aids. For people with visual impairments, Descriptive Listening Devices (DLD) are available upon request.
data.petsDescription: Pets are not allowed into the park theater with the exception of service animals. A service animal is defined as “any dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability." Dogs are the only animals that can be used as a service animal except for miniature horses.
data.locationDescription: The park's orientation film is played in the visitor center theater. There are two separate entrances into the theater. One entrance roughly ten feet from the front desk requires the use of two steps to access, while another entrance into the front of the theater is roughly 25 feet from the front desk but is accessible for people using wheelchairs, walkers, or other assisted mobility devices.
data.longDescription:
Learn About the Man Who Saved the Union and Promoted Civil Rights for All

Everyone loves watching orientation films at national park sites, right? Well, this one doesn't disappoint! "Ulysses S. Grant: A Legacy of Freedom" traces Grant's life from his boyhood in Ohio through his last battle against cancer and a race against time to finish writing his personal memoirs. Produced in 2014, this film summarizes Grant's military service in the American Civil War and provides new insights into his two terms as President of the United States. Some visitors like to start their experience by watching the film, while others prefer to tour White Haven and watch the film afterwards. In any case, there's never a bad time to watch this informative film. 

The orientation film is 22-minutes long and is shown in the visitor center theater every half hour on the top and bottom of each hour. The first showing starts at 9:00AM and the last begins at 4:30PM. In the rare occassion of a special event taking place in the park theater, the film can also be shown on 65" television screen in the visitor center classroom.
data.durationDescription: The park orientation film is 22-minutes long.

data.title: Explore Exhibits About "When The Home Front Became The Front Line"
data.shortDescription: View the museum exhibits at the Visitor Center to learn about Cold War history and the role of the Minuteman Missile in United States nuclear deterrence

images.altText: Visitors view bright exhibits

data.seasonDescription: The museum exhibits are indoors and can be enjoyed year round.
data.accessibilityInformation: The exhibit space is level-surfaced, dimly lit, and gets as narrow as 36 inches. Loud noises overlap one another. Open captioning is present on every film. Service animals are welcome. Please contact park staff with any questions or for accommodations.
data.ageDescription: All ages are welcome, but to get the most out of the experience we suggest Junior Ranger booklets as accompaniment for visitors under 12.
data.petsDescription: Only service animals are permitted in the visitor center.
data.timeOfDayDescription: The museum exhibits can be explored when the Visitor Center is open. Check the days and hours of operation before your visit.
data.locationDescription: The Visitor Center is just north of Interstate 90 at exit 131.
data.longDescription:
Walk through the Cold War when you explore the exhibits at the visitor center. Learn about how the war shaped the home front into the frontlines, created a new league of soldiers, and influenced technological development across the world.

Start reading about the evolution and escalation of nuclear weapons, then transition into the Minuteman Missile’s part in the story. Meet the missileers and experience the home front. Touch part of the Berlin Wall and view propaganda from both sides of the war. Widen your understanding of the arms race before learning about de-escalation. Before exiting the exhibit space, leave a mark on the park by recording your opinions in our log book.
data.durationDescription: Time in the museum exhibits depends on how thoroughly you read the labels and examine the visuals.

Ranger Recommendation
 

The Priest Rock Cabin is about 8 miles from Port Alsworth, and the Joe Thompson Cabin is about 13 miles from Port Alsworth, both on Lake Clark. Seasoned kayakers can paddle from Hardenburg Bay, weather permitting. Visitors can also acquire a water taxi or floatplane to get these spots. Learn more about transportation on our Directions page.

The Joe Thompson Cabin is also the trailhead to the Portage Creek trail. The trail is 3.25 miles in length and travels up to the tundra of Lach Mountian. Visitors to the Priest Rock Cabin can access this trail via boat. The trail is open to the public and can be accessed without reservation to the Joe Thompson Cabin.

data.title: Daemonelix Trail
data.shortDescription: Hike a one-mile trail back in time to the day of the paleocaster, a dry land beaver, and paleosoils, fossilized dirt from the time this landscape was formed. Look out over the vast, open table lands that define the high plaines east of the Rocky Mountains.

images.altText: Looking down on trail from an overlook.

data.seasonDescription: Cooler seasons are best, but the trail can be enjoyed year round. Prepare for the heat with a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water for your entire party. If you have pets please take water for them too.
data.petsDescription: Pets are allowed as long as they are on a leash no more than 6 feet, you remove your pets waste, respect wildlife, and stay on the trail.
data.activityDescription: This is a one-mile hike on a solid surface trail through a rugged landscape. Interpretive signs teill the story of a prehistoric landscape. You can view encased fossils of the paleocaster, a dry land beaver. Elevation offers you a grand view across high plains tables and the Agate Springs Ranch.
data.locationDescription: Daemonlix Trailhead, located on the Park Road, just after turning off NE 29.
data.longDescription:
This one-mile (1.6 km) trail at the west end of the park offers visitors a tour through through time. In addition to a dry land beaver's curious spiral burrows, the Daemonelix or Devil's Corkscrew, visitors see ancient sand dunes and fossil grassland soils called paleosols. From the number and concentration of their now petrified homes, paleontologists know that the paleocastor, the dry land beaver, formed and lived in colonies much like present-day prairie dogs.

From the Daemonelix Trail's highest point, visitors can look out over not only James H. Cook's historic Agate Springs Ranch but also the vast, open tablelands that form the northern terminus of the High Plains east of the Rocky Mountains.

data.title: Fossil Hills Trail
data.shortDescription: Hike to University (left) and Carnegie Hills. The 2.7-mile Fossil Hills Trail allows visitors to walk up to and see the famed early 1900s quarries. From these quarries, paleontologists recovered some of the world's best preserved and most complete fossilized Menoceras, Moropus, and Dinohyus skeletons.

images.altText: The sun illuminates the fossil hills with a dark, stormy sky in the background.

data.seasonDescription: Prepare for summer heat with a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water for your entire party.
data.petsDescription:
Pets are allowed as long as you follow the BARK Ranger principles:
  • Bag your pets waste
  • Always wear a leash
  • Respect Wildlife
  • Know where you can go.
Please stay on the trail. Be sure to take plenty of water for you and your pet.
data.activityDescription: From the visitor center, the trail crosses the Niobrara River and its wetlands, passes through ecologically intact short- and mixed-grass prairie, and then loops around University and Carnegie Hills.
data.locationDescription: This 2.7-mile (4.3-km) wheelchair-accessible paved trail begins at the visitor center.
data.longDescription:
This 2.7-mile (4.3-km) wheelchair-accessible paved trail begins at the visitor center. From the visitor center, the trail crosses the Niobrara River and its wetlands, passes through ecologically intact short- and mixed-grass prairie, and then loops around University and Carnegie Hills. It was on these hills that future local rancher James Cook discovered fossilized bones in the mid 1880s. Excavations didn't commence until nearly twenty years later, following a 1904 visit by Olaf A. Peterson, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Signs along the trail point out and discuss a variety of historic and geologic features; others identify the names of plants, including flowers and grasses.

 

About midway between the visitor center and Fossil Hills is an unpaved one-mile side trail that leads west to Harold J. Cook's homestead cabin. Restored to what it looked like in 1910, while Harold and his wife Eleanor still lived there, the "Bone" cabin was used after 1914 as the temporary residence for scientists who worked the fossil quarries. The American Museum of Natural History's lead excavator, Albert "Bill" Thomson, lived there whenever conducting field work in the bonebed in the late 1910s and early 1920s.

data.title: End of the Trail Lewis and Clark Commemorative Statue
data.shortDescription: This Lewis and Clark statue is located within the Lewis and Clark National Historic Park in Seaside, Oregon.

images.altText: lewis and clark statue with buildings in the background

tags: lewis and clark national historic trail
data.locationDescription: This Lewis and Clark statue is located within the Lewis and Clark National Historic Park in Seaside, Oregon. This historic park represents one of the camping sites during the expedition and also commemorates the west end of the trek led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark.
data.longDescription:
The End of the Trail Lewis and Clark Commemorative Statue is a bronze statue of Captains Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, along with Lewis’ dog, Seaman. The statue was sculpted by Stanley Wanlass and commemorates the Corps of Discovery journey to the Oregon coast.

Read more: https://lewisandclark.travel/nomination/the-end-of-the-trail-lewis-and-clark-commemorative-statue/
